title: Bible Workbook Press
subject: Torts
stem:
Lydia owns a small private print shop that sells Bible-study workbooks. The shop’s press gives off a faint hum, even though Lydia installed state-of-the-art acoustic panels. The shop operates only on weekdays and only during daylight hours. Peter lives next door and works a night shift. When Peter comes home in the morning, he cannot sleep because of the hum from the shop. Other residents in the area do not notice the hum.

Does Peter have a viable nuisance claim against Lydia?
call: Does Peter have a viable nuisance claim against Lydia?

choices.A: No, because Peter is unusually sensitive to noise during the day.
choices.B: No, because Lydia’s shop operates only during the day.
choices.C: Yes, because the hum is heard beyond the boundaries of Lydia’s shop.
choices.D: Yes, because Lydia’s operation interferes with Peter’s quiet use and enjoyment of his property.

rightExplanation:
A is correct.

Gold Key: Private nuisance requires a substantial and unreasonable interference judged against ordinary use and ordinary community expectations. A plaintiff cannot win on a nuisance claim where the harm exists only because of the plaintiff’s unusual sensitivity.

Silver Key: Do not stop at “interferes with quiet use and enjoyment.” In a nuisance array, look for the community-impact facts. Here, the hum is faint, the shop uses acoustic panels, it operates only in normal daytime hours, and ordinary neighbors do not notice it. Peter’s problem comes from his night-shift schedule, not from an ordinary-person-level nuisance.

wrongExplanations.B: The daytime schedule helps Lydia, but it is not the deciding reason. If the daytime noise were loud enough to substantially and unreasonably disrupt ordinary neighbors, daylight-only operation would not automatically defeat nuisance. B answers with the wrong element.
wrongExplanations.C: Sound traveling past Lydia’s property line is not enough by itself. A nuisance claim needs a substantial and unreasonable interference. Boundary crossing proves only a starting fact.
wrongExplanations.D: This is the dominant trap. It uses the right nuisance vocabulary, but it stops too early. Gold Key: “Quiet use and enjoyment” is only part of the private nuisance frame; the interference must also be substantial and unreasonable. Silver Key: when one choice says “interferes with quiet enjoyment,” check whether the stem shows ordinary-community impact or only a sensitive-plaintiff fact. Here, only Peter is affected.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: “Only during the day” is a true fact but not the dispositive nuisance question. It does not answer whether the interference is substantial and unreasonable for ordinary residents.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: “Heard beyond the boundaries” proves only some external effect. It does not complete the nuisance test.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: “Interferes with quiet use and enjoyment” is the attractive half-truth. It omits substantial + unreasonable + ordinary-community impact.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: A. The stem’s unusual-sensitivity facts match the credited answer.

studentScript: Nuisance needs more than any interference. The stem screams one-person sensitivity: faint hum, sound panels, daytime only, neighbors do not notice. Cut the partial yes answers. A.

A.signal: Most fact-engaged answer: it uses Peter's special night-shift sensitivity and the ordinary-neighbor comparator.
A.lawyer: Correct under private nuisance doctrine because harm caused only by unusual sensitivity is not substantial/unreasonable interference as measured by ordinary community expectations.

B.signal: The answer uses a true timing fact but ignores the ordinary-neighbor/sensitivity facts that decide the claim.
B.lawyer: Daylight operation does not automatically defeat nuisance if the interference is otherwise substantial and unreasonable.

C.signal: The answer proves only that the hum leaves Lydia's property, not that it is substantial and unreasonable.
C.lawyer: Private nuisance requires substantial and unreasonable interference, not merely a perceptible effect beyond the defendant's boundary.

D.signal: The answer says the nuisance words but omits the required limiter. The stem gives ordinary-neighbor facts that point the other way.
D.lawyer: Interference with use and enjoyment is not enough unless the interference is substantial and unreasonable; unusual sensitivity defeats the claim.

goldKeys.statement: Private nuisance requires substantial and unreasonable interference judged against ordinary community expectations; a claim based only on the plaintiff’s unusual sensitivity fails.
goldKeys.trigger: Faint condition + reasonable operation + ordinary neighbors do not notice + only plaintiff is bothered because of special schedule/sensitivity.
goldKeys.unlocks: Defeats the quiet-enjoyment half-truth and boundary-crossing half-truth.
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 821D, 821F, 822; Layton v. Yankee Caithness Joint Venture; Cornell Wex nuisance.

silverKeys.statement: When an answer says only 'interferes with quiet enjoyment,' look back for community-impact facts before calling it nuisance.
silverKeys.trigger: A nuisance answer uses broad quiet-enjoyment language while the stem says ordinary residents do not notice.

remediation.title: Quiet enjoyment is not enough
remediation.signal: The answer says 'interferes with quiet use and enjoyment' but the stem marks the plaintiff as unusually sensitive.
remediation.studentMove: Ask: would ordinary neighbors be substantially and unreasonably bothered?
remediation.tinyRule: Nuisance needs ordinary substantial interference, not one-person sensitivity.
remediation.trap: Picking D because it sounds like the nuisance element.
